testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians on Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Out of 301 Indians, reports made on 140: 54 held their land (10 with mortgages), 84 (60%) sold all land, 2 sold part. Of 105 Indians assessed: some classed good/fair, some same, some worse/poor. 77 Indians' land money disposition tracked. Recommended forcing responsibility on younger educated Indians while protecting old. Proposed capitalizing tribal property and buying out individuals' interest.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Assessment of fee patent Indians' condition
testimony.key_claims: Majority of fee patent Indians financially worse off. Most have very little inclination for work and little business experience. If all Indians given full control, 95% would be paupers in less than three years. Fee patent Indians cannot compete with average white man. Doubted whether giving any Indian fee patent without first learning their ability was wise.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Policy recommendations for fee patents
testimony.key_claims: Percentage of Indians who made good considerably smaller than failures. Full-bloods more capable and dependable than mixed-bloods. Recommended individual case examination, holding at least 40 acres inalienable as homestead. Older uneducated Indians not capable of fee patents. Most Indians incapable of farming more than 80 acres. Full-bloods would give better account of freedom than mixed-bloods if judiciously given. Mixed-blood failures showed full-bloods the quality of men assuming tribal leadership.

testimony.witness_title: Field Matron, St. Xavier, Crow Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Individual case reports of fee patent Indians
testimony.key_claims: Provided detailed individual cases: Joseph Cooper sold land, lives in tent. Henry Reid sold land, bought automobile. Thomas LaForge has patent but not sold land. Ralph Saco sold land, lost car and land. Ben Gardner sold land near oil well cheaply. Mary Takes The Gun has not sold. Amy Scott lost cattle ranch through mortgages. Olive R. Venne mortgaged home, items sold at sheriff's sale. Mary Humphrey benefited from citizenship. Two Indians who died had mortgaged places. Richard Wallace did not want a patent.

testimony.witness_title: Baptist Missionary, Lodge Grass, Crow Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Opinion on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Not in favor of turning all Indians loose at once but major portion would benefit from being cut off from government control. Indians will never learn to paddle own canoe on government transport. Most Crows with patents don't make good use of land or money but follow natural human course. Old Indians should remain wards. Some Crows refused citizenship to escape paying taxes. Some Indians should be forced to accept citizenship. Citizenship should be conferred as soon as possible on all except old Indians.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Tulsa, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Status of fee patent Indians in Cherokee and Creek territory
testimony.key_claims: Can think of only a few fee patent Indians in district holding lands and farming. Some who recently received patents have taken no action. In Tulsa, Creek and Washington counties, practically all half-bloods turned loose. About 100 Indians of more than half-blood turned loose through competency commissions. About 25 through departmental removal. Large percentage of latter made good use of property, more successful than average white man. Half-bloods had all restrictions on surplus allotments removed by Act of Congress, very small percent retained lands.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Durant, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Five Civilized Tribes property handling and competency policy
testimony.key_claims: Department's intention is betterment of race but red tape and theoretical methods cause more dependency. No distinction made between various tribes. Five Civilized Tribes never rebelled, follow every vocation. Not in favor of blanket removals. Worker Indians more successful than educated ones without work ethic. About 60% released from competency commission sold or mortgaged property. About 80% doing better than before release. Question whether Indian better off with restricted land he won't work or having sold it and compelled to work. Recommended unconditional removal for able-bodied Indians age 21-35 with eighth grade education. Cited inefficiency of three-tier bureaucratic process for restriction removal. Recommended protecting homestead 40 acres. Restrictions to be automatically removed in 1931.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, United States Indian Service, Shawnee, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Case of Mack Johnson, Kickapoo Indian
testimony.key_claims: Mack Johnson given patent to 40 acres worth $3000-$4000, his only remaining property except quarter interest in 80 acres. Land sold, money spent, mortgage pending on team, tools, stock. Sold mortgaged property, took money to Mexico, died there leaving wife and small children destitute. Missionary and white neighbors furnishing food. Agent who recommended patent bore larger blame for putting him out of business. Indians see agent as responsible for their ruin.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, formerly Standing Rock, North Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: History and results of patent-in-fee issuance at Standing Rock
testimony.key_claims: About 600 patents-in-fee issued at Standing Rock beginning with mixed-bloods prior to 1915. Very few early recipients retained land; became involved in mortgages that consumed resources. Only one Indian personally known who regained allotment after mortgaging. 1916 issuance to mixed-bloods who were as educated and competent as white people - practically all land disposed of. Many women married to white men immediately disposed of lands. Competency Commission dealt with those successful in industrial work and returned soldiers - fair percentage retained lands. Children allotted 50-70 miles from parents had no use for distant land and sold for practical reasons, often wisely spending money on cattle and improvements.
